items.prompt: What role does a port number play, given that an IP address already identifies a machine?
choices: Ports are redundant with IP addresses and serve no separate purpose
A port identifies which specific program on that machine should receive the data
A port encrypts the connection
A port determines the physical location of the server
items.explanation: L1 states this directly — the IP address gets data to the right machine, and the port gets it to the right program running on that machine.
items.reference:
192.168.1.10:443 → HTTPS server

192.168.1.10:5432 → same machine, different program (PostgreSQL)

Why: one machine can run many programs, each on its own port.
items.learnMore:
Machine, then program

IP address and port work together as a two-level address — machine first, then which specific program on it — the same way a street address and an apartment number narrow down a delivery.

Common mistake

Assuming an IP address alone is enough to reach a specific program running on a machine.

items.prompt: Can two completely different programs run on the same machine, each reachable at the same IP address?
choices: No, only one program can ever be reachable per machine
Yes — each is bound to its own port, so the same IP address with different ports reaches different programs
Yes, but only if they're both web servers
No, this requires two separate physical machines
items.explanation: L1's example shows exactly this — the same IP address with different ports (443 vs 5432) reaches two entirely different programs.
items.reference:

Why: one machine can run many programs, each on its own port.

items.prompt: What does TCP actually guarantee delivery of?
choices: A stream of discrete, complete messages
An ordered, reliable stream of BYTES — not a stream of messages
Nothing — TCP makes no delivery guarantees at all
Exactly one 'data' event per application-level write
items.explanation: L1 is explicit — TCP guarantees an ordered, reliable byte stream, with no concept of message boundaries at all.
items.reference:
TCP delivers ORDERED, RELIABLE BYTES.

It does NOT preserve message boundaries.

Why: one write can split into multiple deliveries, or multiple writes can coalesce into one.
items.learnMore:
A byte stream, not a message stream

This is the single most important fact about TCP for anyone writing socket code — every message-boundary bug in this unit traces back to forgetting it.

Common mistake

Assuming TCP treats application-level writes as discrete units that arrive intact.

choices: Yes, this always indicates a network malfunction
No — TCP explicitly allows both splitting one write across multiple deliveries and combining multiple writes into one
Yes, but only on unreliable networks
No, but only for UDP, not TCP

Yes — TCP can combine multiple writes into one delivery, just as it can split a single write across multiple deliveries
Yes, but only if both programs are on the same machine
No, this only happens with UDP

items.prompt: Since TCP doesn't preserve message boundaries, whose responsibility is it to define them?
choices: The operating system's networking stack
The application layer — the program using the socket has to define its own framing scheme
The router hardware between the two machines
This is impossible and message boundaries can never be recovered
items.explanation: L1 is explicit — since TCP doesn't preserve boundaries, the application itself has to define an explicit framing scheme on top of the raw byte stream.
items.reference:
A wire protocol = an agreement about message boundaries and structure, layered on TCP's raw byte stream.

Why: TCP guarantees bytes; the application has to define what a 'message' means within them.
items.learnMore:
Protocols are boundary agreements

Any wire protocol — HTTP, a custom chat protocol, anything — is fundamentally an agreement about how to find message boundaries and structure inside a raw byte stream.

Common mistake

Expecting the network layer to preserve application-level message structure with no explicit framing scheme.

items.prompt: Per L2's sequence diagram, what are the three steps of the TCP handshake, in order?
choices: ACK, SYN, SYN-ACK
SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK
SYN, ACK, SYN-ACK
SYN-ACK, SYN, ACK
items.explanation: L2's diagram shows the exact order — client sends SYN, server responds SYN-ACK, client confirms with ACK.
items.reference:
1. Client → Server: SYN

2. Server → Client: SYN-ACK

3. Client → Server: ACK

Why: both sides agree the connection exists before any application data flows.
items.learnMore:
Connection-oriented

The handshake is why TCP is 'connection-oriented' — both sides explicitly establish and agree on a connection before exchanging any application-level message, unlike UDP.

Common mistake

Assuming a TCP connection begins transmitting application data before the handshake completes.

items.prompt: Per L2, how does newline-delimited framing determine a message boundary?
choices: By counting exactly 100 bytes per message
Each message ends with a newline character; the reader scans for that byte to find boundaries
By waiting exactly one second between messages
By requiring every message to be the same length
items.explanation: L2 describes newline-delimited framing exactly this way — each message ends with '\n', and the reader splits on that character.
items.reference:
Newline-delimited: each message ends with '\n'

Length-prefixed: each message preceded by its own byte length

Why: two common, different ways of encoding message boundaries into the byte stream.
items.learnMore:
Two common schemes, different tradeoffs

Newline-delimited is simple but breaks if the content itself can contain the delimiter byte; length-prefixed avoids that but requires reading and tracking a length field.

Common mistake

Choosing newline-delimited framing without considering whether the message content could ever contain a newline.

items.prompt: Per L2, how does length-prefixed framing determine a message boundary?
choices: By searching the byte stream for a special delimiter character
Each message is preceded by its exact byte length, so the reader knows precisely how many bytes to read
By requiring a fixed delay between messages
By encrypting each message separately
items.explanation: L2 describes length-prefixed framing exactly this way — a length value precedes each message, telling the reader exactly how many bytes constitute it.
items.reference:
Newline-delimited: each message ends with '\n'

Length-prefixed: each message preceded by its own byte length

Why: two common, different ways of encoding message boundaries into the byte stream.
items.learnMore:

No, but only for newline-delimited framing
items.explanation: L2 states this as a general rule — buffering across events is required regardless of which specific framing scheme is used, since TCP never guarantees message-per-event delivery.

items.prompt: Why should a framer drain ALL complete messages from its buffer on each 'data' event, not just the first one found?
choices: It doesn't matter — at most one message can ever arrive per event
Multiple complete messages can be coalesced into a single 'data' event, so stopping after the first would silently drop the rest
Draining multiple messages at once is slower than one at a time
This only matters for length-prefixed framing
items.explanation: Since TCP can coalesce multiple writes into one delivery, a framer must keep extracting complete messages in a loop, not stop after the first one found.
items.reference:
'{"a":1}\n{"b":2}\n' arriving as ONE chunk → two complete messages

Why: a framer using "if" instead of "while" would silently lose the second message.
items.learnMore:
Loop, don't check once

A framer's buffer-draining logic needs a loop specifically because TCP delivery patterns are unpredictable — any single 'data' event could contain zero, one, or several complete messages.

Common mistake

Using a single boundary check per data event instead of looping until the buffer has no more complete messages.

It would silently lose any messages beyond the first one found in a chunk containing multiple complete messages
It would throw an explicit error
It would process messages faster with no downside
items.explanation: This is exactly L3's warning — an `if` instead of `while` silently drops additional messages present in the same chunk.
